live_note: Day six, Monday morning: the story moved in two directions overnight. The one vendor account of a successful intrusion is withdrawn: Unit 42 retracted its Oct 23 report of an AI-agent-like attacker taking credentials at a European government agency, saying on Oct 25 (2:15 p.m. PT) that it 'is unable to confirm that initial access is associated with the specific PHP2Shell CVEs'; the attack happened 'in the context of a vulnerable PHP application', which is what led it to the PHP2Shell call. This index carried that report as its siren for two days and now records the retraction. In the other direction, BleepingComputer reported on Oct 26 (05:19 ET) that the flaws are 'successfully exploited in the wild': a honeypot run by Adel Karimi, Perplexity's detection and response lead (the same 0x4D31 report this index logged Oct 25), recorded confirmed code execution against Apache mod_php on PHP 8.4.26, and Expel's Marcus Hutchins calls it 'by far the highest quality confirmation of in-the-wild php2shell exploitation I've seen so far'. That is proof the public technique works against a real unpatched server, not a victim: Dataminr says activity before it was 'limited to scanning, fingerprinting, and use of non-working exploits, with no known compromises'. Still no organization confirmed breached by name; still no PHP release since Oct 21 (php.net read Oct 26 morning); still no CISA listing (the KEV feed opened directly at 07:08 ET: version 2026.10.23, 1,756 entries). New numbers: TU Delft's live dashboard, 41,907 exploitation requests from 586 IPs in 68 countries since Oct 21; VirusTotal, 5.1 million exposed PHP hosts, 3.8 million with an attackable port. Restorations: most Nepal government sites are back, KB Kookmin's tablet-branch service resumed in Korea. A researcher won the StealMyBitcoin challenge against an unpatched server Oct 25 and published a proof of concept.
